summary: Describes the environment and goals for using the IEEE 802.15.4e Time-Slotted Channel Hopping MAC in low-power and lossy networks. It lists an initial set of problems that IETF work must address to run IP over such networks.

plainLanguage.summary: TSCH lets wireless devices communicate in synchronized time slots and change radio channels between transmissions. This RFC lists the scheduling and network-management problems that another layer must solve to use TSCH with IP.

subtitle: The scheduling and management problems to solve when using TSCH for low-power IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) defines how synchronized devices communicate, but it does not define how to build and maintain their communication schedules.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the low-power and lossy network setting and lists problems for a higher-layer scheduling entity, including joining, routing, resource allocation, timing, and security.
tldr.outcome: It is an initial problem statement for using TSCH with IPv6 networking; it does not specify a scheduling protocol.

sections.title: TSCH in Low-Power Networks
sections.content:
Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) is a medium access control mode for IEEE 802.15.4 wireless networks. It uses synchronized time slots and channel hopping to support low-power operation and communication over links affected by interference.

TSCH can sit below an IPv6 protocol stack for low-power and lossy networks. The IEEE specification defines how a node follows a schedule, but leaves the creation and maintenance of that schedule to another function.
sections.plainLanguage: TSCH coordinates wireless devices so they know when to transmit, receive, or sleep. The standard does not say how the network creates or updates that schedule.

sections.title: Schedules, Cells, and Synchronization
sections.content:
A TSCH schedule tells each node what to do in each time slot and which neighbor to contact. A scheduled cell is one communication opportunity between neighbors. Multiple cells can be grouped into a bundle to provide more opportunities for traffic between the same nodes.

Nodes must stay synchronized and use the same timing information to communicate in their scheduled cells. Channel hopping changes the frequency used over time, while the schedule determines which nodes communicate and when.
sections.plainLanguage: A schedule is a repeating plan that tells each device when to send, listen, or sleep. Devices also need to keep their clocks aligned so they use the same planned times.

sections.title: Problems for the Scheduling Function
sections.content:
The logical link control (LLC) function described by the RFC needs to help nodes discover a network, join it, and remain synchronized. It also needs to gather topology information and ensure that scheduled cells exist along the multi-hop routes chosen by the routing protocol.

The LLC must manage how many cells neighbors receive, how nodes negotiate changes, how traffic and buffers are handled, and how time-sensitive traffic meets its deadlines. The RFC also identifies secure joining, key management, and coordination between scheduling approaches as open problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A scheduling function must help devices join, stay synchronized, and get communication slots along their routes. It must also manage changing traffic, deadlines, and security.

sections.title: Different Ways to Build a Schedule
sections.content:
The RFC describes centralized and distributed scheduling as possible approaches. A central path computation element can assign resources using a network-wide view. Alternatively, neighboring devices can monitor traffic and negotiate changes to their cells.

Different approaches may suit different networks, and more than one may operate in the same network. The scheduling function therefore needs ways for these approaches to coexist and for nodes to exchange information about their schedules.
sections.plainLanguage: A central controller can assign communication slots, or neighboring devices can negotiate them. The RFC identifies coexistence between these approaches as a design problem.
